transcript.text: Indesit washer dryer washes fine but the drying cycle doesn't get warm at all, clothes come out cold and wet after 2 hours. Model is XWDE 96 something.

Because there is no warmth at all after two hours, the leading possibility is a fault in the drying heating circuit — commonly the drying heater, its thermostat or thermal cut-out. However, it is worth ruling out a restricted fluff/water path and an overloaded or poorly spun load first, as these can cause poor drying and can contribute to an overheat cut-out operating. 1. Check the laundry before drying. It should have completed a proper fast spin and be damp rather than dripping. A washer-dryer also dries less than it can wash, so try a small load only. If a small, well-spun load dries normally, there is no heater failure; it was loading/spin-related. 2. With the machine switched off and unplugged, clean any accessible fluff filter. If there is a pump filter behind the lower front flap, put towels and a shallow tray down and open it slowly, as water may come out. Clear fluff and debris, then refit it securely. A blockage can restrict the drying/condensing water path. Then try a timed drying cycle with just a couple of well-spun towels. If the drum air and laundry remain completely cold, rather than merely drying slowly, that points to the drying heater circuit and an engineer will need to test the heater, thermostat/thermal cut-out and associated wiring safely. Do not dismantle the machine or test mains components yourself.

The load was about 4kg and the drum and door glass were stone cold the whole time, so I don't think it's just slow drying. There's no burning smell and nothing has tripped. Is there anything else worth checking before I call an engineer?

Yes — there are two worthwhile checks before booking someone, but the completely cold drum makes a drying-heater circuit fault the leading cause. No burning smell and no tripped electrics do not rule that out; an open heater element or thermal cut-out commonly fails quietly. 1. Check the cold-water tap feeding the machine is fully open, and—with the machine switched off and unplugged—check its inlet hose and drain hose are not kinked or crushed. Washer-dryers generally use cold water during drying to condense moisture and send it away. A supply or drain restriction can cause poor drying, although it would more often give warmth with damp clothes rather than a stone-cold drum. 2. Complete the pump-filter check already outlined, if you have not done so. A fluff-blocked filter can restrict the drying condensate path and may also contribute to an overheat cut-out operating. If the hoses are clear, water supply is on, and the filter is clear/cleaned but a timed drying cycle still stays cold, it is no longer a loading or slow-drying issue. An engineer should test the drying heater, thermostat/thermal cut-out, wiring and then the control board if those prove sound. Internal access and electrical testing are not a sensible owner repair here.

I can hear water trickling at the back during drying, so I assume the tap is on. I haven't looked at the hoses or the pump filter yet. Could a bad hose or filter really make the drum completely cold, or is that still more likely the heater?

The water trickling at the back makes it more likely that the condenser water supply is present. So the drying heater circuit remains the more likely cause: the heater element itself, its thermostat, or a thermal cut-out. A blocked filter can still matter because a restriction can contribute to a thermal cut-out operating, so it is worth checking before arranging a repair. 1. With the machine switched off and unplugged, check the pump filter behind the lower flap. Put towels and a shallow tray down first, then open it slowly. Remove any fluff/debris and refit it securely. A heavily blocked filter supports a condensate/drain restriction; if it is clear, that makes the heater circuit more likely. 2. Pull the machine forward only if safe to do so, and check the cold inlet hose and drain hose are not crushed or sharply kinked. The drain hose and its sink/standpipe connection should also be free-draining. A clear hose and filter, combined with completely cold drying, points strongly to the heater/thermal protection side. If those are clear, book an appliance engineer rather than continuing to run two-hour drying cycles. They will need to test the drying heater, thermostat/thermal cut-out, wiring and, only if those are sound, the control board. Internal access and electrical testing are not sensible owner checks here.

candidates: Drying heater circuit fault — heater element, thermostat or thermal cut-out (high)
Restricted airflow/condensing path or fluff blockage (medium)
Load too large for the drying capacity or laundry not spun sufficiently first (medium)
